title: Master Class | 1.B3!! Nimzo-Larsen | Chess Speedrun | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: It seems contradictory, but you don't play b3 to occupy most of the centre — you do it to attack the centre with pieces. b3, d6 is fine, nothing wrong with that move, provided
he accompanies it with e5. The bishop to b2.

e5 is a legitimate way to play. But h5 is obviously completely unhinged — and funnily, a5 in this position is a legitimate line grandmasters have played, and I've faced it over the board; the idea is to undermine the pawn chain with a4, though I think White is probably slightly better, and the best move against a5 is actually c4, which isn't easy to play unless you've analysed it.
The point against a4 is not to take it, which ruins your pawn structure, but to go b4, then a3, and then this pawn ends up being a big weakness — just a little theoretical side note.
So the bishop to b2, h5, e3, a5 — we decided to play it
more simply with a3, but in the over-the-board game I play c4 here, just so you know.
So a3, and again the idea against a4 is to go
b4. Now, who can explain to me
why the move bishop to b5 with check doesn't win
Not the bishop to d7, although the bishop to d7 is possible — the move is c6. Just remember this little trap:
if you capture with your bishop, this bishop
doesn't have a passageway back to b3 — so that's a good thing to remember.
The bishop to b5, c6 is fine. Now you might look at this and say, wait a second, what if I take the pawn first?
The point here is that Black will not do this and blunder his exchange.
But the fact is these pawns are horrible.

Black doesn't even have to win the pawn back — it's just that you're saddled with these weaknesses the rest of the game, and it's well worth a pawn that Black is probably going to win back anyway. So, the knight to f6, the knight to f3, c6, and now we occupy the centre with d4, the knight to d7, the bishop comes out actively to d3, and the move b5 is the straw that broke the camel's back. If I were Black here, I'd go g6 or e6 and just rush to develop my pieces. Now we just say, let's step on d4. He correctly played e6, because if he had just developed his bishop — who can tell me what White should do? Black is almost losing already, and it has to do with him playing h5, which weakens the g6-square, something you'd notice immediately if you're tactically sharp. We go e5, and after g5, what's the key move? It's going to be absolutely painful, just crunching through his position. e6.
